conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: The answer is no.** The strongest long-term, placebo-controlled evidence does not support saw palmetto's superiority over placebo for improving BPH symptoms.

**Key Evidence:**

1. **STEP Trial (NEJM, 2006):** A one-year, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial randomizing 225 men with moderate-to-severe BPH to saw palmetto extract (160 mg twice daily) or placebo. The study found that "saw palmetto was not superior to placebo for improving urinary symptoms and objective measures of benign prostatic hyperplasia." ([https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085))

2. **CAMUS Trial (JAMA, 2011):** A multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 369 men using escalating doses of saw palmetto (up to 960 mg/day) over 72 weeks. This trial also failed to show benefit over placebo, even at doses higher than standard. ([https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1104439](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/1104439))

3. **Cochrane Review (2012):** The updated Cochrane systematic review by Tacklind et al. reflected the impact of these large negative trials, tempering earlier optimism from smaller, methodologically weaker studies. ([https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD002281.pub3/full](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD002281.pub3/full))

4. **Wikipedia summary:** States plainly that "there is no clinical evidence that it is effective for this purpose." ([https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saw_palmetto_extract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saw_palmetto_extract))

While some older meta-analyses of smaller trials suggested modest symptom improvement, the two largest and most rigorous long-term placebo-controlled trials—STEP and CAMUS—both found no significant benefit over placebo. The current best evidence does not support the claim that saw palmetto improves BPH symptoms in the longer term compared to placebo.
